title: Given a sorted array of integers and a target value, return the index of the target if it is present, otherwise return minus one. The algorithm must run in logarithmic time.
shortTitle: Classic Binary Search: Find a Target in a Sorted Array in O(log n)
keyPoints: Binary search divides a sorted array in half each step, finding or rejecting the target in O(log n) time.
Compute the midpoint as low + (high - low) / 2 to avoid integer overflow.
The loop condition is while (low <= high) so a single-element window is still checked.
Always exclude mid from the next window with low = mid + 1 or high = mid - 1 to prevent infinite loops.
Binary search requires the array to be sorted as its fundamental precondition.
For an array of one million elements, binary search needs at most 20 comparisons.
Binary search generalizes to searching on answer spaces for optimization problems.

s1_definition.oneliner: Compare the middle element to the target, then discard the half that cannot contain it, repeating until found or the window closes.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Binary search** – a divide-and-conquer algorithm on a sorted array that repeatedly halves the search interval by comparing the target to the middle element.
- **Midpoint calculation** – use `mid = low + (high - low) / 2` instead of `(low + high) / 2` to avoid integer overflow on large arrays.
- **Loop condition** – `while (low <= high)` ensures a single-element window is checked before the search concludes.
- **Discard logic** – if `arr[mid] < target`, the target is to the right, so `low = mid + 1`; if `arr[mid] > target`, the target is to the left, so `high = mid - 1`.
- **Time complexity** – O(log n) because each comparison halves the remaining range; O(1) space for the iterative form.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank of India has a ledger of accounts sorted by account number and Rajesh needs to find a specific one. Instead of reading every line, he opens the ledger in the exact middle. If the middle number is too high, the account must be in the left half, so he throws away the right half. If too low, he throws away the left half. He keeps halving until he lands on it, checking only a handful of pages even in a ledger of a million accounts.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Binary search is the fundamental logarithmic-time algorithm for finding a target in a sorted array. You keep two bounds, low and high, that frame the current search window, and on each step you look at the middle element. If it equals the target you are done. If the middle is smaller than the target, the answer can only be to the right, so you move low past the middle. If the middle is larger, the answer can only be to the left, so you move high below the middle. Every comparison discards half the remaining range, so searching a million elements takes only about twenty steps.

Two implementation details separate a correct solution from a buggy one. First, compute the midpoint as `low + (high - low) / 2` rather than `(low + high) / 2`, because the naive form can overflow a 32-bit integer when the array is very large. Second, always exclude the middle from the next window using `+1` and `-1`, and loop while `low <= high` so that a single-element window is still checked. Getting these details wrong causes either infinite loops or missed elements.

In Rajesh's work at the National Bank of India, binary search powers the account authentication system. When a customer logs in, the system looks up their account number in a sorted array of millions of active accounts. Binary search confirms the account exists in about 20 comparisons, which meets the strict latency requirements that a linear scan never could.

The deeper reason binary search matters is that it generalizes well beyond arrays. The same halving idea applies to searching on an answer space for optimization problems: finding the minimum EMI that pays off a loan, the minimum capacity to ship packages, or the smallest rate that satisfies a constraint. Mastering the classic version, including the overflow-safe midpoint and the correct loop invariant, pays off far beyond simple array lookups.

Remember one sentence: binary search halves the search window on each step, finding any target in a sorted array of n elements in at most log2(n) comparisons.
